title: Synopsys:“Silicon-To-Systems”
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

How Synopsys built the simulation infrastructure that lets engineers test chip designs for errors, before they are sent to the factory for manufacturing.

Synopsys occupies an essential but often overlooked position in the global semiconductor industry: it sells the tools that prove complex chip designs will work before manufacturers commit millions of dollars to fabrication. Founded in 1986 by engineers from General Electric, the company pioneered logic synthesis, automating the conversion of high-level circuit descriptions into verified gate-level designs. Its growth from $130,000 in 1987 revenue to $7.05 billion in fiscal 2025 reflects the relentless rise of chip complexity.

The company solves a genuine coordination problem. As transistor counts increased, no design team could continue verifying chips manually, while maintaining proprietary tools duplicated enormous research costs. Synopsys created a neutral, shared toolchain serving competing designers without manufacturing chips itself. Its integration with foundry process-design kits makes its software part of the infrastructure required to launch new manufacturing nodes.

This infrastructure creates enduring value, but also substantial lock-in. Customers embed Synopsys tools, scripts, workflows, and expertise into multiyear development programs, making migration to Cadence or Siemens EDA expensive. Competition among these three vendors constrains pricing, especially when new projects begin, although that discipline weakens once customers commit to a platform. Open-source alternatives remain promising but are not yet adequate for leading-edge designs.

Synopsys has also expanded beyond traditional electronic design automation. Its artificial-intelligence tools explore vast design possibilities, while its $35 billion acquisition of Ansys extends verification into thermal, structural, and fluid simulation. The combined company can model chips as parts of complex physical systems rather than isolated circuits.

Bottom line: Synopsys strongly qualifies as coordination infrastructure. It helped make Moore’s Law commercially achievable by preventing design complexity from becoming the industry’s limiting factor. Yet its neutrality is imperfect: switching costs concentrate power, and American export controls restrict access for Chinese firms, showing that essential infrastructure can remain vulnerable to corporate dependence and geopolitical policy.
